title: What We Talk About When We Talk About Logs: Understanding the Effects of Dataset Quality on Endpoint Threat Detection Research
abstract: Endpoint threat detection research hinges on the availability of worthwhile evaluation benchmarks, but experimenters' understanding of the contents of benchmark datasets is often limited. Typically, attention is only paid to the realism of attack behaviors, which comprises only a small percentage of the audit logs in the dataset, while other characteristics of the data are inscrutable and unknown. We propose a new set of questions for what to talk about when we talk about logs (i.e., datasets): What activities are in the dataset? We introduce a novel visualization that succinctly represents the totality of 100+ GB datasets by plotting the occurrence of provenance graph neighborhoods in a time series. How synthetic is the background activity? We perform autocorrelation analysis of provenance neighborhoods in the training split to identify process behaviors that occur at predictable intervals in the test split. Finally, How conspicuous is the malicious activity? We quantify the proportion of attack behaviors that are observed as benign neighborhoods in the training split as compared to previously-unseen attack neighborhoods. We then validate these questions by profiling the classification performance of state-of-the-art intrusion detection systems (R-CAID, FLASH, KAIROS, GNN) against a battery of public benchmark datasets (DARPA Transparent Computing and OpTC, ATLAS, ATLASv2). We demonstrate that synthetic background activities dramatically inflate True Negative Rates, while conspicuous malicious activities artificially boost True Positive Rates. Further, by explicitly controlling for these factors, we provide a more holistic picture of classifier performance. This work will elevate the dialogue surrounding threat detection datasets and will increase the rigor of threat detection experiments. 112 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Introduction From its very beginnings, host intrusion detection re- search has been impeded by the availability of evaluation data. Industry is understandably reluctant to publish their own event logs, which may contain proprietary information, while generating benchmark datasets that are realistic in scale and complexity is tedious and unrewarding for researchers. When individual researchers or funded programs invest in dataset creation, design considerations often begin and end with the sophistication of the attack behaviors. For example, the DARPA Transparent Computing program [37] hired professional penetration testers to conduct well-documented attack engagements. However, attacks comprise only a small proportion of a dataset, and it is much more difficult to understand the rest of the dataset's contents. While attacks are exciting and important to consider, we currently lack the means to holistically evaluate the quality of endpoint threat detection datasets. Even conceptualizing the contents of a log dataset, which may contain hundreds of gigabytes of system events (or more), is a challenge. Neglecting the contents of background activity is especially problematic for anomaly-based intrusion detection methods, a popular topic of academic research, because classification performance in anomaly detection is a function of the rela- tionship between typical (benign) and atypical (attack) data. A more critical assessment of our benchmark datasets would help us to better evaluate the merit of threat detection systems, and may even help to explain why so many promising- looking methods have failed to transition to practice. In this work, we propose a battery of principled and generalizable metrics for measuring the quality of endpoint detection datasets. Our approach builds on established threat investigation approaches using data provenance, which inter- prets audit logs as a causal relationship graph describing the history of system execution. We present novel methods for quantifying and analyzing the properties of these graphs to facilitate comparison across datasets. Our contributions are organized as a series of questions that we should be asking when we “talk about logs” - that is, when we carefully consider what these datasets can actually tell us about threat detection systems: What activities are in the dataset? ( §3) Even reasoning about the contents of a large intrusion detection dataset can prove challenging. We demonstrate that a “bird's eye view” of the data can be obtained by tracking the occurrence of each process neighborhood in the provenance graph as a time series, enabling high-level reasoning about the background activity in a dataset. Using this approach, we recover undocumented information about popular datasets such as machine downtime and other experimental artifacts. How synthetic is the background activity? Our approach recovers the periodicity of process neighborhoods in the provenance graph through autocorrelation. We find that we can predict the occurrence of nearly 60% of all process neighborhoods in the time series with a less than 10% false negative rate. How conspicuous is the attack activity? ( §5) Especially in anomaly detection, the (dis)similarity between typical and atypical data dictates classification performance. An attack that is extremely dissimilar to background activity lacks covertness and may be trivial to identify. To provide a measure of these effects, we compare process neighborhoods observed in the training (pre-attack) period to malicious neighborhoods observed in the test period. We discover a high degree of variance in attack covertness between datasets, ranging from 99% (E3 Trace) all the way to 0% (ATLASv2). To demonstrate the value of these metrics, we conduct an exhaustive evaluation where we manipulate dataset quality metrics and observe the impact on state-of-the-art threat detection systems R-CAID [29], FLASH [58], and KAIROS [11] (§6), as well as a commodity-off-the-shelf Graph Neural Network (GNN). We go on to discuss how our findings should inform the generation of future datasets ( §7), then consider prior work on security dataset metascience ( §8) before concluding ( §9). 2. Endpoint Threat Detection Datasets Since the earliest intrusion detection research, classifi- cation performance evaluation required benchmark datasets. We summarize public datasets for endpoint (i.e., traditional computer) intrusion detection research in Table 1. Qualitative descriptions of the datasets can be found in Section A. Here, we call attention to the disparities in ground truth labeling practices between datasets. On the finer-grained TABLE 2: Dataset attack labeling statistics, including the number of attack processes recovered and the proportion of attack processes to all processes per dataset. Dataset # Attack % Attack E3 Cadets 2821 2.6 E3 FiveDirections 9982 4.2 E3 Theia 47 0.02 E3 Trace 86 0.001 ATLASv2 H1 149 1.0 ATLASv2 H2 17 0.1 OpTC Host 201 11 0.07 OpTC Host 501 50 0.3 side, datasets label malicious processes or every malicious entity (including processes) implicated in the attack. Other datasets report only coarse-grained information about which log-file of system-wide activity contains the attack, i.e., both benign and malicious processes are present in the log. Within these categories, the precision and completeness of labels still vary. For example, DARPA TC and OpTC provide only qualitative attack descriptions that require trial-and-error to identify the specific log entities. ATLAS identifies only a subset of the malicious entities (2-3) per attack, when there are actually many more. Standardizing Ground Truth Labels. As IDS become more advanced, the potential for researcher intent to influence evaluation results becomes a greater concern. Individual experimenters are often left to make their own decisions as to which events/entities should be designated as malicious, creating a conflict of interest. It also complicates comparing datasets, which is a central goal of this work. To address these shortcomings, we make use of a standardized and evidence-based method of labeling in which all processes on the attack chain are labeled as malicious . In our approach, the human is still responsible for identifying the root cause(s) and terminal impact(s) of an attack - in other words, where the attack begins and ends - but not intermediary steps. We then use Fang et al.'s method of identifying a concise attack chain by taking the intersection of the forward trace from the root cause(s) and the backwards trace from the impact(s) [20]. All processes in this chain are labeled as Malicious, reducing experimenter degrees of freedom. However, due to the imprecision of provenance graphs, it is often the case that benign entities appear to have causal relationships with attack entities. It is unreasonable to expect a classifier to label these entities as malicious, because they are not, but it is also unreasonable to expect a classifier to ignore the apparent causal relationship to the attack chain. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce a Contaminated label to denote samples that should be withheld from the test set. We identify contaminated processes by conducting a forward trace from the root cause(s) of the attack, marking everything that is not already labeled as Malicious as Contaminated. It is unreasonable to expect a classifier to label these entities as malicious, because they are not, but it is also unreasonable to expect a classifier to ignore the apparent causal relationship to the attack chain. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce a Contaminated label to denote samples that should be withheld from the test set. We identify contaminated processes by conducting a forward trace from the root cause(s) of the attack, marking everything that is not already labeled as Malicious as Contaminated. General statistics about the number of implicated attack processes from this method are shown in Table 2. Our labels, as well as a more detailed description of our labeling 113

Endpoint threat detection research hinges on the availability of worthwhile evaluation benchmarks, but experimenters' understanding of the contents of benchmark datasets is often limited. Typically, attention is only paid to the realism of attack behaviors, which comprises only a small percentage of the audit logs in the dataset, while other characteristics of the data are inscrutable and unknown. We propose a new set of questions for what to talk about when we talk about logs (i.e., datasets): What activities are in the dataset? We introduce a novel visualization that succinctly represents the totality of 100+ GB datasets by plotting the occurrence of provenance graph neighborhoods in a time series. How synthetic is the background activity? We perform autocorrelation analysis of provenance neighborhoods in the training split to identify process behaviors that occur at predictable intervals in the test split. Finally, How conspicuous is the malicious activity? We quantify the proportion of attack behaviors that are observed as benign neighborhoods in the training split as compared to previously-unseen attack neighborhoods. We then validate these questions by profiling the classification performance of state-of-the-art intrusion detection systems (R-CAID, FLASH, KAIROS, GNN) against a battery of public benchmark datasets (DARPA Transparent Computing and OpTC, ATLAS, ATLASv2). We demonstrate that synthetic background activities dramatically inflate True Negative Rates, while conspicuous malicious activities artificially boost True Positive Rates. Further, by explicitly controlling for these factors, we provide a more holistic picture of classifier performance. This work will elevate the dialogue surrounding threat detection datasets and will increase the rigor of threat detection experiments. 112 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)
